title: 04 Howl Hill Weekender: neo-brutalist festival hero
strengths: The poster idea is real: Big Shoulders Display at full width with a hard offset shadow, bordered-cell nav, the date and 'BUY TICKETS' as cells
Copy has a voice and facts: '41 loud bands, three tiny stages, a lake to cool off in... No VIP. Ever.'; the lineup ticker names bands that sound like bands
Three colours only (yellow, blue, black) with strong tonal contrast; Space Grotesk for small text is a good second face
slop_signals: Four stickers on one screen: the '41 bands, 3 stages' circle, the tilted 'WEEKENDER' label, the 'SOLD OUT' stamp and the 'ALL AGES' starburst; the starburst is the most-used badge shape there is
The poster card is generic line art: a yellow moon with craters, three four-point stars, black hills with white peaks
Two crossing tickers with star separators; one marquee is a device, two is a pattern
Two buttons ('GET TICKETS £89' filled, 'PLAY LINEUP' outlined) in the stock pair
Neo-brutalism (flat yellow, 3 px borders, hard shadows) is now a default theme in AI page builders; Mobbin shows almost no shipped festival site in it
fixes: Keep one sticker (the date) and remove the starburst and the stamp; put 'sold out' as a struck-through line in the ticket button
Replace the moon-and-hills card with something only Howl Hill has: a hand-drawn site map of the three stages and the lake, or last year's crowd photo in a bordered cell
One ticker, the lineup, running under the headline; move the practical notes (jumper, trains, kids) into plain text
Reduce the shadow offset on the display word so it reads as print, not as a CSS effect

references.what: Condensed display across the full width with the date set small above it, over a real photograph; proves the type alone carries it
One marquee band with an object sitting on it and one rotated date sticker; the same ingredients used once each
Flat yellow with thick black outline art and a bordered header; its art is a drawn idea (peppers, a sun face), not stock shapes
Shipped festival pages lean on crowd photography and one line of type; a reminder of what the audience sees elsewhere
